nameStory: Potter's Grass Spider gets its name from the naturalist who first described it, combined with its preference for grassy habitats. Like a potter shapes clay into useful vessels, this spider crafts distinctive funnel-shaped webs that serve as both home and hunting trap.
description: Potter's Grass Spider is a medium-sized brown spider that builds distinctive sheet webs with funnel retreats in grassy areas. These spiders have elongated bodies with a somewhat flattened appearance and long, sturdy legs built for speed. They typically measure about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch in body length, with females being noticeably larger than males.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for a flat, sheet-like web stretched between grass stems with a distinctive funnel or tube-shaped retreat at one corner where the spider hides - the web feels silky but substantial when accidentally brushed

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated, somewhat flattened brown body with a slightly glossy appearance and visible spinnerets (silk-producing organs) extending from the rear abdomen

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Incredibly fast runner that darts across its web to catch prey, then quickly retreats to its funnel - they rarely leave their webs during daylight hours

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Brown to grayish-brown coloration with subtle darker stripes or chevron patterns on the abdomen that can be hard to see without close inspection

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized with females reaching about three-quarters of an inch in body length while males stay closer to half an inch - legs span roughly two inches

habitat: Potter's Grass Spiders favor open grassy areas including meadows, field edges, suburban lawns, and roadside ditches throughout New England. They particularly like areas where tall grasses and low shrubs create good anchor points for their horizontal webs. You'll often find their webs stretched between grass clumps in sunny to partially shaded locations with some moisture nearby.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and begin web-building activity as grasses grow tall enough to support their sheet webs, typically late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most visible and spiders are actively hunting - this is the best time to observe their lightning-fast prey capture behavior.
seasonality.fall: Mating season brings increased activity as males venture away from webs to seek females, and egg sacs are produced before the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off with hard frosts, while eggs overwinter to hatch the following spring - webs become tattered and abandoned.

funFact: Potter's Grass Spiders are so fast they can run across their webs and grab flying insects out of mid-air before the prey even realizes it's been caught - their reaction time is measured in milliseconds, making them some of the quickest hunters in the spider world.
confusionNotes: Often confused with wolf spiders found in similar grassy habitats, but remember the web rule: if you see a funnel web, it's a grass spider - wolf spiders don't build webs and hunt by chasing prey on foot instead.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being native to North America, Potter's Grass Spider has somehow managed to establish populations in Ukraine, Russia, and Kyrgyzstan, making it one of the few New England spiders to become an intercontinental traveler - likely through accidental human transport.
compareHints: Potter's Grass Spider is very difficult to distinguish from its close relative the Dark-legged Grass Spider without examining fine details under magnification - both build similar funnel webs in grassy areas and have nearly identical behavior patterns. The main difference lies in subtle leg coloration patterns that require expert identification, so many field observers simply refer to them collectively as 'grass spiders.'

relatedSpecies.distinction: Utah Funnelweb Spiders are very similar to Potter's Grass Spider and Dark-legged Grass Spider, all sharing the same web-building style and general appearance.
Dark-legged Grass Spiders are distinguished from Potter's Grass Spider by their notably darker leg coloration and slightly smaller size.
